items.title: The Enterprise XDR Implementation Roadmap: From Planning to Measurable Outcomes
items.summary: Key Takeaways Follow a practical XDR implementation roadmap to unify detection, automate response, improve SOC workflows, and measure security outcomes. Understand baseline performance before implementation: Measure current detection, investigation, containment, analyst effort, and coverage so improvement can be proven. Design the architecture around data quality: Validate timestamps, identity context, asset attribution, retention, ingestion latency, and data completeness. Deploy XDR in controlled waves: Establish the platform foundation first, connect network and endpoint telemetry next, then expand into identity, cloud, SaaS, OT, and IoT. Automate response according to operational risk: Begin with enrichment and evidence collection before introducing high-impact containment actions. Operationalize XDR inside the SOC: Redesign workflows, assign clear ownership, and train analysts by role, so the platform changes how investigations are performed. Measure implementation success through outcomes: Track coverage, detection accuracy, investigation speed, containment time, evidence quality, and business value. Attackers do not respect the boundaries between your endpoint platform, network controls, identity infrastructure, cloud environment, and SIEM. They now use those boundaries. That gap is one reason enterprises are investing in Extended Detection and Response. But purchasing an XDR platform does not automatically close it. A successful XDR implementation requires more than connecting telemetry sources and enabling default detections. It requires a deliberate operating model that brings architecture, detection engineering, investigation, response, and measurement together. This roadmap explains how to move from initial planning to an operational XDR program that delivers measurable outcomes, with a particular focus on how Fidelis Elevate ® supports that transition. What is XDR Implementation? XDR implementation is the process of integrating network, endpoint, identity, cloud, application, threat intelligence, and other security telemetry into a coordinated detection, investigation, and response architecture. The XDR implementation process usually include: Defining security outcomes and priority use cases Assessing existing tools and visibility gaps Designing the target data and integration architecture Deploying sensors, agents, collectors, and integrations Normalizing and correlating security telemetry Engineering and validating detections Automating approved response actions Embedding XDR into SOC workflows Measuring detection, investigation, and response performance Continuously tuning and expanding the platform The objective is not simply to put more data into another console. It is to create an operating layer that can follow an attack across security domains, preserve the evidence analysts need, and coordinate response before the adversary completes the next stage of the intrusion. Why XDR Implementations Underperform Most unsuccessful XDR projects fail because the organization treats implementation as a technology rollout rather than a security operations transformation. Common warning signs include: Data Without a Use Case: Telemetry is connected before teams define what threats or attack paths they need to detect. Coverage That Hides Blind Spots: Endpoint coverage looks strong on paper, while unmanaged and high-risk assets remain invisible. Perimeter-Only Network Visibility: Traffic is monitored at the edge, leaving east-west movement and internal attack activity unobserved. Identity Context Stays Isolated: Identity and Active Directory activity are not correlated with endpoint and network evidence. Security Tools Lack Clear Roles: SIEM, SOAR, EDR, NDR, and threat intelligence tools overlap without defined responsibilities or data flows. Default Rules Replace Detection Engineering: Out-of-the-box correlation rules are enabled without tuning them to the organization’s environment, assets, and threats. Automation is Introduced Too Early: Response actions are automated without business impact analysis, approval controls, or rollback procedures. Investigations Remain Fragmented: Analysts continue moving between disconnected tools instead of investigating through a unified XDR workflow. Success Is Measured by Activity: Teams track alerts, events, and integrations instead of improvements in detection, investigation, and containment. Wrong XDR implementation results in technically integrated security that remains operationally fragmented. That outcome is especially dangerous now. Verizon’s 2026 DBIR [1] found that vulnerability exploitation had become the leading breach entry point, accounting for 31% of breaches. The same research found third-party involvement in 48% of breaches. Automation in XDR: Reduce Manual Effort. Strengthen Cyber Defense Early Threat Discovery Automating Incident Response Playbooks Automating Cyber Terrain Mapping Read the Guide The Enterprise XDR Implementation Roadmap An effective roadmap should deliver value incrementally. Trying to connect every source, migrate every control, and automate every response in one release usually creates a long implementation cycle with no clear production milestone. Key Takeaways
  • Follow a practical XDR implementation roadmap to unify detection, automate response, improve SOC workflows, and measure security outcomes.

Attackers do not respect the boundaries between your endpoint platform, network controls, identity infrastructure, cloud environment, and SIEM. They now use those boundaries.

That gap is one reason enterprises are investing in Extended Detection and Response. But purchasing an XDR platform does not automatically close it.

A successful XDR implementation requires more than connecting telemetry sources and enabling default detections. It requires a deliberate operating model that brings architecture, detection engineering, investigation, response, and measurement together.

This roadmap explains how to move from initial planning to an operational XDR program that delivers measurable outcomes, with a particular focus on how Fidelis Elevate® supports that transition.

What is XDR Implementation?

XDR implementation is the process of integrating network, endpoint, identity, cloud, application, threat intelligence, and other security telemetry into a coordinated detection, investigation, and response architecture.

The XDR implementation process usually include:

  1. Defining security outcomes and priority use cases
  2. Assessing existing tools and visibility gaps
  3. Designing the target data and integration architecture
  4. Deploying sensors, agents, collectors, and integrations
  5. Normalizing and correlating security telemetry
  6. Engineering and validating detections
  7. Automating approved response actions
  8. Embedding XDR into SOC workflows
  9. Measuring detection, investigation, and response performance
  10. Continuously tuning and expanding the platform

The objective is not simply to put more data into another console. It is to create an operating layer that can follow an attack across security domains, preserve the evidence analysts need, and coordinate response before the adversary completes the next stage of the intrusion.

Why XDR Implementations Underperform

Most unsuccessful XDR projects fail because the organization treats implementation as a technology rollout rather than a security operations transformation.

Common warning signs include:

  • Data Without a Use Case: Telemetry is connected before teams define what threats or attack paths they need to detect.
  • Coverage That Hides Blind Spots: Endpoint coverage looks strong on paper, while unmanaged and high-risk assets remain invisible.
  • Perimeter-Only Network Visibility: Traffic is monitored at the edge, leaving east-west movement and internal attack activity unobserved.
  • Identity Context Stays Isolated: Identity and Active Directory activity are not correlated with endpoint and network evidence.
  • Security Tools Lack Clear Roles: SIEM, SOAR, EDR, NDR, and threat intelligence tools overlap without defined responsibilities or data flows.
  • Default Rules Replace Detection Engineering: Out-of-the-box correlation rules are enabled without tuning them to the organization’s environment, assets, and threats.

  • Investigations Remain Fragmented: Analysts continue moving between disconnected tools instead of investigating through a unified XDR workflow.
  • Success Is Measured by Activity: Teams track alerts, events, and integrations instead of improvements in detection, investigation, and containment.

Wrong XDR implementation results in technically integrated security that remains operationally fragmented.

That outcome is especially dangerous now. Verizon’s 2026 DBIR[1] found that vulnerability exploitation had become the leading breach entry point, accounting for 31% of breaches. The same research found third-party involvement in 48% of breaches.

items.title: Critical Red Hat Kubernetes SSRF Flaw Exposes Internal Services Across Managed Clusters
items.summary: Red Hat has disclosed CVE-2026-66794, a high-severity Server-Side Request Forgery vulnerability affecting the cluster-proxy-addon component in Multicluster Engine for Kubernetes. The issue carries a CVSS v3.1 score of 9.3. It could allow unauthenticated remote attackers to reach otherwise inaccessible services running across managed Kubernetes clusters. The vulnerability exists in a user-facing route exposed by the cluster proxy add-on . According to Red Hat, the route does not properly enforce authentication and authorization before forwarding requests. An attacker who can access this endpoint can manipulate URL path segments to make the proxy send requests to arbitrary services in managed clusters. This behavior is classified as CWE-918, or SSRF. Rather than directly attacking an internal service from the internet, an attacker abuses the vulnerable proxy as an intermediary. Red Hat Kubernetes SSRF Flaw The proxy appears to be trusted by internal infrastructure, allowing requests to cross boundaries that network controls, service exposure restrictions, or cluster segmentation would normally protect. In a multicluster Kubernetes deployment , this could be particularly serious. Management-plane components often have connectivity to services distributed across several managed clusters. If exposed via a vulnerable route, attackers may access internal APIs, retrieve sensitive application data, identify reachable internal endpoints, or interact with services never intended to be externally available. For example, an attacker could manipulate a request path so that the affected proxy contacts an internal service in a managed cluster. If that service returns configuration data, tokens, debugging details, or application responses without requiring separate authentication, the attacker may obtain information useful for further intrusion. The actual impact depends on which services the proxy can reach and what security controls those services enforce. Red Hat rated the issue Important rather than Critical despite the high 9.3 CVSS score. Its analysis states that the confirmed impact is unauthenticated SSRF, not remote code execution. The vendor identified high confidentiality impact, low integrity impact, and no demonstrated availability impact. The affected components are multicluster-engine/cluster-proxy-addon-rhel9 and multicluster-engine/cluster-proxy-rhel9 within Multicluster Engine for Kubernetes. At the time of publication, Red Hat listed both as affected and did not identify associated security errata. Organizations should immediately restrict network access to the user-facing cluster-proxy-addon route. Red Hat recommends applying firewall rules or equivalent network controls to ensure that only trusted networks and authorized sources can connect to the exposed port. Administrators should also review route exposure, inspect proxy access logs for unusual path patterns, and identify sensitive internal services reachable from the management environment. Prevent incidents due to slow investigations. items.title: Hackers Hide Malware Code Inside English Words to Infect Windows Users
items.summary: A new Windows malware campaign is hiding malicious code inside ordinary English words, making the payload look less suspicious during analysis. The technique is being used to deliver Amatera Stealer, an information-stealing threat that targets sensitive data stored on infected systems. The campaign relies on ClearFake, a long-running operation that compromises legitimate websites and places fake CAPTCHA checks over real pages. Visitors are told to complete a verification step, but the prompt actually guides them into running a malicious command through the Windows Run dialog. Analysts at GenDigital identified the new loader, called WordlistLoader, and found that it rebuilds hidden shellcode from a list of common English words. The approach gives attackers another way to conceal code while keeping the infection chain focused on human error rather than a software vulnerability. Examples of compromised websites serving ClearFake’s FakeCaptchas (Source – GenDigital) GenDigital said in a report shared with Cyber Security News (CSN) that the immediate risk falls on Windows users who follow unexpected browser instructions, especially requests to press Win+R, paste clipboard content, and hit Enter. Such ClickFix-style lures have become a common delivery method for information stealers because they persuade victims to launch the malicious command themselves. Hackers Hide Malware Code Inside English Words WordlistLoader stores its next-stage code as a sequence of plain English words. Each word corresponds to a single byte through a build-specific list containing 256 unique words. The loader processes the word sequence, finds each word’s position in the list, and writes the matching byte into memory. In simple terms, a harmless-looking list of words becomes executable malware only after the loader translates it back into machine code. This makes static inspection harder because security tools and analysts may initially encounter readable text instead of an obvious block of shellcode. Infection chain (Source – GenDigital) GenDigital also found a modified WordlistLoader variant that swaps the English-word list for UUID values. In that version, each UUID represents a 16-byte chunk of code, showing that the operators can change the encoding method without changing the broader execution flow. The loader is not limited to hiding code. Before it launches the reconstructed payload, it checks whether another copy is already running, attempts to restore altered system-module functions, and interferes with Windows event logging. These actions are designed to make security monitoring and investigation more difficult. The campaign begins on hacked websites where attackers inject JavaScript into otherwise legitimate pages. The injected code can use EtherHiding, a technique that retrieves further malicious content from a blockchain smart contract, before presenting a fake CAPTCHA to the visitor. Readers can see how similar ClickFix campaigns use EtherHiding to turn browser visits into malware delivery attempts. Fake CAPTCHA Leads to Amatera After a visitor clicks the fake “I’m not a robot” prompt, the site copies a command to the Windows clipboard. The victim is then instructed to open the Run dialog and paste it, unknowingly starting a hidden command process that accesses a remote WebDAV share and launches a malicious DLL through rundll32. This delivery method is particularly effective because it uses built-in Windows components rather than requiring a traditional exploit. A related WebDAV rundll32 ClickFix technique shows how attackers continue to adapt trusted system tools for malware execution. WordlistLoader eventually launches Amatera, also known as ACR Stealer. Amatera has been actively updated and includes stronger code obfuscation, methods to avoid security hooks, and routines aimed at recovering protected browser encryption keys. WordlistLoader’s wordlist and the shellcode encoded as English words (Source – GenDigital) Previous reporting on the Amatera stealer web campaigns documented its use of compromised websites and fake verification prompts. The stealer can target browser-held information, including credentials and data that may be valuable for account takeover or further fraud. Its newer versions also use techniques intended to interact with 64-bit browser processes and obtain keys protected by Chromium’s Application-Bound Encryption feature. Users should treat any CAPTCHA, browser warning, or website verification request that asks them to open Run, Terminal, Command Prompt, or PowerShell as malicious. Legitimate CAPTCHA services do not require users to paste commands into Windows. Organizations should also monitor for unusual rundll32 activity, clipboard-triggered command execution, WebDAV connections, and visits to compromised sites. Similar fake CAPTCHA malware attacks underline why user awareness remains a critical part of endpoint defense. The WordlistLoader delivers Amatera through ClearFake campaigns, combining deceptive website overlays with layered code hiding and defensive evasion. items.title: Hackers Are Turning Claude, ChatGPT and Copilot Into Bait for Real Malware
items.summary: Cybercriminals are increasingly using trusted artificial intelligence names as a shortcut to infect users with malware. Fake download pages, browser extensions, search ads and shared AI conversations are being used to make harmful files and commands look legitimate. The campaigns target people looking for popular AI tools, coding assistants and productivity features. A victim may search for an installer, click a sponsored result, or install an apparently useful extension, only to receive a backdoor, password-stealing malware or a browser hijacker instead. Sophos researchers identified the trend after reviewing a year of managed detection and response investigations. Of 38 confirmed cases involving hostile AI activity, 30 involved software impersonation, showing that criminals are mainly abusing AI brands rather than using AI itself to run attacks. The impact reaches both individuals and organizations. Stolen browser sessions, saved passwords, private files and cryptocurrency wallet data can give attackers a foothold into wider business systems. Sophos said in a report shared with Cyber Security News (CSN) that the campaigns also exploit a difficult reality: users are more likely to trust an installation prompt when it carries a familiar AI name. Claude, ChatGPT and Copilot Into Bait for Real Malware Claude was the most frequently abused lure in Sophos’ review, appearing in 26 cases. Attackers used fake Claude, ChatGPT and Microsoft Copilot pages to distribute malware through malicious ads, poisoned search results and domains designed to resemble legitimate vendor websites. Many incidents relied on InstallFix, a variation of the ClickFix social-engineering method. Instead of presenting a fake error page, the attacker offers a polished installation guide that tells visitors to copy and run a command. That command then downloads or launches the real payload. Fake Claude ‘InstallFix’ site (Source – Sophos) In one case, a fake Claude site directed victims to execute an mshta command that retrieved a Windows application package named claude or claude.msixbundle . A second command ran code directly in memory and attempted to hide its activity inside a browser process. This same approach has become a familiar entry point in wider malware operations. A recent ClickFix malware delivery campaign similarly used fake verification pages to convince Windows users to execute commands themselves, turning normal user actions into the start of an infection. Sophos also observed LummaStealer delivered through AI-branded infrastructure, as well as a fake Claude Setup.zip archive that planted a harmful libcef.dll file. Another repackaged claude.exe acted as a loader, while a more developed fake site used DLL sideloading to install the previously undocumented Beagle backdoor. The strongest early defense is still simple: obtain AI tools only from confirmed vendor domains. That advice matters because fake pages can closely copy official branding, layouts and download flows. Extensions and Trusted Platforms Abused The abuse does not stop at installers. Researchers found AI-themed browser extensions that presented themselves as useful assistants while collecting browser data and communicating with attacker-controlled servers. Since extensions can be granted broad access to sessions and stored credentials, they are especially attractive to data thieves. In one investigation, four customers installed a fake Perplexity extension that hijacked searches and sent browsing telemetry in real time. The extension redirected searches through perplexity-ai[.]online and displayed a landing page after installation, creating the appearance of a normal AI service. Uncensored Qwen3.5 build promoted in The Gentlemen ransomware group’s leaked internal chats (Source – Sophos) The danger is not limited to obscure download sites. Sophos found that one fake extension appeared in the Chrome Web Store with a 4.7-star rating, 67 reviews and 10,000 installs. That apparent credibility can reduce suspicion, much like the malicious AI extensions targeting enterprises that harvested conversations and browsing data. Attackers have also begun placing their lures on trusted services. In several macOS campaigns, the trick moved from fake brand pages to shared conversations hosted on legitimate ChatGPT infrastructure. Victims were then instructed to paste Terminal commands, a technique also seen in abused Claude shared chats used to spread information-stealing malware. Organizations should audit AI-related browser extensions, verify the publisher before installation and remove extensions that are not necessary. Security teams should also monitor for unusual command execution, suspicious PowerShell activity and browser processes launching system utilities, because the behavior remains detectable even when the initial lure uses a trusted AI brand. AI dependencies deserve the same supply-chain controls as other software packages. Sophos documented poisoned packages and malicious plugins that fetched remote code, warning that automated development tools could shrink the time between a malicious package being published and executed. items.title: CyberPanel Pre-Auth RCE Chain Lets Attackers Gain Server Shell via AI Scanner Flaws
items.summary: Security researchers have disclosed a critical pre-authentication RCE chain in CyberPanel that could let attackers gain a shell on vulnerable hosting servers without valid credentials. The attack combines weaknesses in the platform’s AI Scanner functionality with stored cross-site scripting and abuse of cron jobs. The issue affects CyberPanel versions earlier than 2.4.4. CyberPanel is a web hosting control panel for managing websites, DNS, email, databases, and server services. Because it serves as a central control plane, a successful compromise can grant attackers broad access to hosted environments. Pentera researchers identified the chain during an analysis of internet-facing hosting panels. The researchers found that CyberPanel contained an unauthenticated AI Scanner endpoint intended to receive scan data from an external service. CyberPanel Pre-Auth RCE Enables Server Shell The endpoint accepted user-controlled scan results and stored them in the application database without properly sanitizing the content. This created a stored cross-site scripting vulnerability tracked as CVE-2026-41472. An attacker could place malicious JavaScript in a forged scan result, but initially faced an important limitation: the request required a valid scan_id. Without a legitimate scan identifier, the application rejected the submitted result. cronCommand is explicitly excluded from security filtering due to its special characters ( source: Pentera ) The missing piece was an exposed debug API endpoint , /api/ai-scanner/list-api-keys. The endpoint could be accessed without authentication and returned information about recent AI scans, including valid scan IDs.. This access-control issue, tracked as CVE-2026-41473, allowed attackers to obtain the identifier needed to submit a malicious scan result. After obtaining a valid scan ID, an attacker could inject JavaScript into the stored scan record. The malicious code would not execute immediately. Instead, it would wait until a CyberPanel administrator opened the AI Scanner results page. When the administrator viewed the poisoned result, the script would run in the administrator’s authenticated browser session . The RCE chain (Source: Pentera) The attack code could then use the administrator’s active session and CSRF token to perform actions on the administrator’s behalf. Pentera researchers demonstrated that the script could silently create a new administrative account. This gave the attacker valid access to the CyberPanel dashboard without needing to steal a password directly. The final stage involved CyberPanel’s cron job management feature. After logging in with the newly created account, the attacker could create a website and associated system user, then abuse cron job functionality to execute a command on the server. Researchers found that the cronCommand parameter could dangerously allow shell command execution. This enabled the attacker to obtain a server shell. Nuclei template to check access to sensitive APIs (Source: Pentera) The chain demonstrates how several individually limited weaknesses can combine to become a full server takeover. The exposed API endpoint leaked data, stored XSS-enabled privilege abuse , and cron job handling enabled command execution. Pentera reported the vulnerabilities to CyberPanel on May 4, 2026. The CyberPanel team reportedly issued fixes within about four hours, including removal of debug endpoints, authentication for callback functionality, and output escaping. Administrators should update CyberPanel to the latest patched release immediately. Organizations unable to patch should turn off the AI Scanner feature and restrict access to /api/ai-scanner/list-api-keys and /api/ai-scanner/test-auth until updates can be deployed. items.title: Police Are Hiding Their Use of Flock Surveillance Cameras
items.summary: A usage policy for Flock license plate reader cameras tells police not to talk about the cameras: When cops use Flock to arrest someone in Wapello County, Iowa, they don’t want them to know. A usage policy for the automated license plate reader cameras in the county tells police, in no uncertain terms, to keep them a secret: “DO NOT MENTION ALPR USAGE TO THE OCCUPANTS OF THE VEHICLE,” the policy document reads. “DO NOT MENTION ALPR USAGE IN YOUR REPORT OR COMPLAINT UNLESS ABSOLUTELY NECESSARY.” This reminds me of IMSI-catchers (Stingray was the most popular) a couple of decades ago. Police would go to even more extremes to hide their usage.

items.title: New “Zombie Card” Flaw Lets Expired Visa Cards Make Contactless Payments
items.summary: Security researchers have demonstrated that an expired credit card is not as dead as most cardholders believe. A new study from the University of Massachusetts Amherst, presented at the 35th USENIX Security Symposium, reveals a practical NFC relay attack dubbed “Zombie Card” that revives expired Visa contactless cards, allowing them to complete real purchases at point-of-sale terminals across multiple US banks. The core discovery is deceptively simple: card expiration in EMV contactless payments is enforced as a transaction policy check performed by the terminal, not as a cryptographic fact baked into the card itself. EMV contactless payment The private keys stored on a chip never expire, and the certificates that authenticate a card during Offline Data Authentication often remain valid well past the card’s printed date to smooth over reissuance periods. That leaves the actual expiry decision resting on a single data field, the Application Expiration Date, which the terminal reads in plaintext and checks locally. Zombie Card Back Online Researchers Raja Hasnain Anwar, Gerard DeCunha, and Muhammad Taqi Raza built a man-in-the-middle relay using two NFC-capable Android phones , one emulating the card near the POS terminal and one emulating the terminal near the physical card, communicating over Wi-Fi. NFC relay This setup lets them intercept and rewrite APDU data exchanged during the transaction’s data-retrieval phase in real time, using nothing more than commodity smartphones. Testing spanned EMV Kernel 2 (Mastercard), Kernel 4 (American Express), Kernel 6 (Discover), and Kernel 3 (Visa). Kernels 2, 4, and 6 detected tampering because expiry-related data is cryptographically bound to signed records or hashed transaction data, so any in-flight edit broke signature verification and killed the transaction. Kernel 3 was the outlier. Experimental setup Its expiration field is excluded from the signed dynamic application data, so flipping a past date to a future one slips past the terminal’s local check without breaking any signature. Making matters worse, Kernel 3 forwards an all-zero Terminal Verification Results field to the issuer, meaning banks never learn that the terminal’s local validation was manipulated. Combined with card-side flags that can force a transaction “online” even when expiry checks fail, this created an open path for an expired card carrying a still-valid Primary Account Number to reach the issuer’s authorization system unchallenged. The team validated the attack in a lab using SumUp terminals and then in the wild at retail and grocery merchants, across five major US banks, using their own expired and replaced cards to avoid any third-party harm. Results diverged by issuer: one bank approved zombie transactions across amounts up to $500 because it validated only the account and cryptogram rather than the specific card instance, while another consistently declined and prompted use of the replacement card. Notably, even a non-expired card that had already been replaced by its issuer continued processing successful payments on the same account. The researchers proposed countermeasures spanning every layer of the payment chain: cryptographically binding expiry data to signed records, forcing consistency checks between the terminal’s expiry field and the value sent to issuers, treating expiration and replacement as explicit issuer-side authorization predicates, and preserving genuine validation results instead of zeroing them out. They disclosed the findings to Visa and affected banks in May 2025, with Visa’s red team still reproducing the attack as of the paper’s acceptance, and no confirmed fixes deployed yet. Until systemic changes land, cardholders should follow standard advice: destroy expired cards by cutting through the chip and magnetic stripe rather than discarding them intact. items.title: 15 Malicious Firefox Extensions Abuse Cloudflare Workers to Exfiltrate Crypto Wallet Secrets
items.summary: Firefox users are facing a coordinated campaign of malicious add-ons that masquerade as cryptocurrency wallets, themes, and simple browser tools. The extensions can trick victims into disclosing recovery phrases, private keys, login details, and clipboard data, placing digital assets and online accounts at immediate risk. Active since at least March 2026, the operation spans 77 Firefox extension identities: 40 confirmed malicious add-ons and 37 deceptive sports-score shells that helped the group blend into the marketplace. Researchers at Socket.dev identified the campaign and provisionally call it Offside Wallet Theft Factory. It also gives operators a cheap way to rotate brands, infrastructure, and deceptive listings. Socket.dev said in a report shared with Cyber Security News (CSN) that reused code, shared infrastructure, deceptive descriptions, and changes to older extension identities point to a repeatable publishing operation. Representative attack flow for the confirmed malicious extensions (Source – Socket.dev) The findings show why an add-on’s stated purpose or modest permission request cannot establish trust. Samples used a notepad or sports application as cover while theft happened inside the extension or on a remote page. 15 Malicious Firefox Extensions Abuse Cloudflare Workers Fifteen of the malicious extensions embedded fake wallet screens or altered wallet code directly in their signed packages. They captured recovery phrases and private keys during wallet creation or import, then sent the data to attacker-controlled Cloudflare Workers deployments. This echoes Cloudflare Workers abuse cases , where a legitimate cloud service is misused to conceal hostile delivery or collection infrastructure. Several variants copied or modified Rabby-derived wallet code but used unrelated, theme-style names. Their implant intercepted new or imported 12-word and 24-word recovery phrases. Other samples presented counterfeit Portal, OKX, or generic Web3 import pages, relying on victims to type their secret rather than searching the browser for it. A recovery phrase can restore a wallet on another device, so an attacker who receives it can take control independently. Deleting the extension may stop additional collection, but it cannot make a disclosed phrase safe again. The 0KX WEB3 listing was live during our analysis and presented the extension as a cryptocurrency wallet (Source – Socket.dev) The risk follows the wallet stealing add-on problem: trust in an apparently useful browser tool becomes the path to account takeover. A separate group of 13 modified Rabby-style extensions took a quieter route. Before the wallet software encrypted and saved its keyring data locally, altered code sent the serialized keyrings to hardcoded HTTP servers. Because the data left first, normal local encryption offered no protection for the copied information. Repurposed Add-Ons Expand the Campaign Seven extensions used a remote-control design built around attacker-managed Supabase projects. One example, 0KX WEB3, advertised wallet features but contained no real wallet functions. Instead, it loaded a remote website in its popup, displayed a decoy notepad when inactive, and opened the supplied page after installation or an update. The remote page asked users to create or import a wallet and then requested a recovery phrase or private key. This staged approach makes review harder because operators can switch an extension between harmless-looking and phishing content without republishing it. It also reinforces lessons from recent extension supply chain attacks , where a later update can change a trusted tool into a data-stealing one. Five more extensions collected credentials and clipboard contents through a hardcoded command-and-control server. Clipboard theft can expose copied passwords, authentication material, wallet addresses, or private keys. Investigators also found 37 add-ons that claimed to provide unrelated utilities but were actually repackaged sports-score applications; nine malicious identities had older sports-score versions before turning into wallet stealers. Users and security teams should remove listed extensions, review add-ons again after every update, and verify publishers through official project channels before installing wallet software. Do not enter a recovery phrase or private key into a browser popup or webpage. Anyone who entered either secret into a suspect extension should treat it as permanently compromised, move assets to a newly created wallet, and replace exposed credentials. Firefox users are facing a coordinated campaign of malicious add-ons that masquerade as cryptocurrency wallets, themes, and simple browser tools.

The extensions can trick victims into disclosing recovery phrases, private keys, login details, and clipboard data, placing digital assets and online accounts at immediate risk.

Active since at least March 2026, the operation spans 77 Firefox extension identities: 40 confirmed malicious add-ons and 37 deceptive sports-score shells that helped the group blend into the marketplace.

Researchers at Socket.dev identified the campaign and provisionally call it Offside Wallet Theft Factory. It also gives operators a cheap way to rotate brands, infrastructure, and deceptive listings.

Socket.dev said in a report shared with Cyber Security News (CSN) that reused code, shared infrastructure, deceptive descriptions, and changes to older extension identities point to a repeatable publishing operation.

Representative attack flow for the confirmed malicious extensions (Source – Socket.dev)

The findings show why an add-on’s stated purpose or modest permission request cannot establish trust. Samples used a notepad or sports application as cover while theft happened inside the extension or on a remote page.

15 Malicious Firefox Extensions Abuse Cloudflare Workers

Fifteen of the malicious extensions embedded fake wallet screens or altered wallet code directly in their signed packages.

They captured recovery phrases and private keys during wallet creation or import, then sent the data to attacker-controlled Cloudflare Workers deployments.

This echoes Cloudflare Workers abuse cases, where a legitimate cloud service is misused to conceal hostile delivery or collection infrastructure.

Several variants copied or modified Rabby-derived wallet code but used unrelated, theme-style names. Their implant intercepted new or imported 12-word and 24-word recovery phrases.

Other samples presented counterfeit Portal, OKX, or generic Web3 import pages, relying on victims to type their secret rather than searching the browser for it.

A recovery phrase can restore a wallet on another device, so an attacker who receives it can take control independently. Deleting the extension may stop additional collection, but it cannot make a disclosed phrase safe again.

The 0KX WEB3 listing was live during our analysis and presented the extension as a cryptocurrency wallet (Source – Socket.dev)

The risk follows the wallet stealing add-on problem: trust in an apparently useful browser tool becomes the path to account takeover. A separate group of 13 modified Rabby-style extensions took a quieter route.

Before the wallet software encrypted and saved its keyring data locally, altered code sent the serialized keyrings to hardcoded HTTP servers. Because the data left first, normal local encryption offered no protection for the copied information.

Repurposed Add-Ons Expand the Campaign

Seven extensions used a remote-control design built around attacker-managed Supabase projects. One example, 0KX WEB3, advertised wallet features but contained no real wallet functions.

Instead, it loaded a remote website in its popup, displayed a decoy notepad when inactive, and opened the supplied page after installation or an update.

The remote page asked users to create or import a wallet and then requested a recovery phrase or private key. This staged approach makes review harder because operators can switch an extension between harmless-looking and phishing content without republishing it.

It also reinforces lessons from recent extension supply chain attacks, where a later update can change a trusted tool into a data-stealing one. Five more extensions collected credentials and clipboard contents through a hardcoded command-and-control server.

Clipboard theft can expose copied passwords, authentication material, wallet addresses, or private keys.

Investigators also found 37 add-ons that claimed to provide unrelated utilities but were actually repackaged sports-score applications; nine malicious identities had older sports-score versions before turning into wallet stealers.

Users and security teams should remove listed extensions, review add-ons again after every update, and verify publishers through official project channels before installing wallet software.

Do not enter a recovery phrase or private key into a browser popup or webpage. Anyone who entered either secret into a suspect extension should treat it as permanently compromised, move assets to a newly created wallet, and replace exposed credentials.

This is especially important given earlier malicious Firefox extension activity, which showed that add-ons can also target passwords and OAuth tokens.

Missing input validation allows unsafe deserialization of stored data without confirming that the supplied content has the expected type. The issue stems from unsafe deserialization of embedded pickle content. Other AI Toolkit flaws could allow lower-privileged users to perform searches with system-level privileges, manage containers and connections without proper authorization , access or delete other users’ experiment history, and modify scheduled searches that run under the search owner’s permissions. Splunk AI Toolkit versions below 6.0.0 are affected by most of these issues, while two flaws affect versions below 6.0.1. items.title: Claude AI Finds SAML Security Flaws That Can Let Attackers Take Over Accounts
items.summary: Security researchers have used Anthropic’s Claude AI to uncover serious flaws in Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) implementations that could allow attackers to bypass authentication and take over user accounts. The findings highlight the persistent security risks created by XML signature processing, inconsistent parser behavior, and custom SAML code. A researcher at Oblique Security built an AI-assisted testing harness around Claude Opus to examine SAML libraries and applications. Rather than directing the model to reproduce known bugs, the system supplied a threat model and let Claude explore how each implementation handled signed XML data. The process separated the discovery of unusual parser behavior from validation, in which the model attempted to create a working end-to-end exploit. Claude AI Finds SAML Flaws SAML is widely used for enterprise single sign-on , allowing an identity provider to send signed authentication assertions to a service provider. However, secure implementation depends on both components interpreting the same XML document in the same way. When signature verification and application logic process XML differently, attackers may be able to supply unsigned identity data that the application mistakenly trusts. The research identified full authentication bypasses in four projects, including Authentik, PHP litesaml/lightsaml, OneUptime, and Java saml-client. In three cases, the issue involved SAML signature wrapping , a long-standing attack class in which an attacker moves or injects XML elements so that a valid signature is verified on a different object. At the same time, the application reads identity information from another. The most notable issue affected Authentik, an open-source identity provider. Tracked as CVE-2026-57580, the flaw allowed an attacker to use an XML comment inside a SAML NameID value. Under certain non-default account-matching modes, Authentik could interpret the value before the comment as a victim’s username or email, even while the signed assertion remained valid. This could link an attacker-controlled external identity to the victim’s account, creating a persistent path to account takeover. Authentik fixed the vulnerability in versions 2026.2.6 and 2026.5.5. Organizations using inbound SAML sources with USERNAME_LINK or EMAIL_LINK matching should verify that they have applied the update. The vendor noted that default unique-identifier matching and outbound SAML provider deployments were not affected. The investigation also uncovered weaknesses outside standard SAML login responses. According to Oblique Security research , signature validation bypasses in authentication requests, attribute queries, and logout operations could enable information disclosure or arbitrary user logouts. Denial-of-service risks were also common. Several libraries accepted attacker-controlled XML documents that could trigger excessive memory usage during signature validation or XML transformation. Such weaknesses are especially dangerous because they can often be exploited before authentication. The findings reinforce a familiar message for identity teams: avoid custom SAML implementations whenever possible. Developers should use mature, actively maintained libraries, strictly validate signed elements, turn off dangerous XML transforms, impose document-size and resource limits, and test identity flows for parser differentials and signature wrapping attacks. AI can accelerate vulnerability discovery, but it can also expose how fragile legacy XML-based authentication implementations remain. Prevent incidents due to slow investigations.
